REJECTIONS UNDER 35 USC SECTION 101

Claims 21-42 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is allegedly directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. Examiner argues the claims are directed to the abstract idea of mental processes and/or certain methods of organizing human activity. Examiner further argues the claims do not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.

Examiner states that "The underlined limitations in claim 21 recite an abstract idea included in the groupings of mental processes and/or method of organizing human activity, connected to technology only through application thereof using generic computing elements".
Applicant submits that amended claim 21 does not recite an abstract idea.

Applicant's claims are directed to systems and methods which fall under the statutory category of a machine or a process, both of which are eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Applicant submits the amended claims should then be analyzed to determine whether they are directed to an abstract idea and if the elements in the amended claims amount to mere instructions applied using generic computer components. Applicant's claims focus on a particular technological environment, namely multi-player video games, not just any game environment, and are directed towards the execution and operation ofmulti-player video games and not to the manipulation of abstract data.

Amended claim 21 pertains to a specific technological system or method for managing gameplay sessions in a multiplayer video game environment which involves coordinated operations across servers and client devices and extending the game map of a multiplayer video game. Although Examiner alleges that certain limitations, like "querying players", might involve abstract ideas, the claim as a whole integrates these operations into a specific technological solution.

Examiner has further states that: "the claimed invention merely applies the judicial exception, or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, or merely uses a computer as a tool to perform the abstract idea (MPEP 2106.05 (f)) and/ or generally links the use of the judicial exception to a particular technology or field of use (MPEP 2106.05 (h)). The claimed computer components are recited at a level of generality and are merely invoked as tool to perform the abstract idea. Simply implementing the abstract idea on a generic computer is not a practical application of the abstract idea."

Applicant would like to bring to the Examiner's attention the Berkheimer memorandum which follows the US Federal Circuit's opinion in Berkheimer v. HP case no. 2017-1437, and clarifies the second step of the Mayo/Alice test, and also revises the examination procedure for rejecting claims on that basis. The memorandum states that the conclusion of whether an element is well-understood, routine and conventional must be based on afactual determination. The memo suggests that a claim recites "significantly more" unless proven otherwise, and states that an additional element is not well-understood, routine or conventional unless the examiner finds, and expressly supports such a rejection in writing. The memo makes clear that such a statement by the examiner will normally require a citation to be provided by the examiner.
Further, the Applicant submits following MPEP Examples supporting the eligibility of
the Applicant's claims:
MPEP Example 39: A method for dynamically adjusting parameters of an operating system based on user behavior was found eligible because it was directed to a technological improvement.

Similarly, Applicant's amended claims provides a concrete system (customization application and gameplay session engine) to achieve a specific improvement in the gameplay experience, including transitioning between bounded and unbounded sessions.

on each of the plurality of client devices, wherein the gameplay session engine is further
configured to:
initiate the bounded gameplay session for all the players;
query a predetermined number of the players to determine if the bounded
gameplay session should be converted to the unbounded gameplay session for all the

MPEP Example 40: A gaming system for managing multiplayer gaming sessions was determined to be patent eligible when it improved the technological field of multiplayer gaming by providing specific rules and mechanisms for interactions. Applicant's amended claims align with this rationale as the claims recite specific, non-generic configurations (e.g., monitoring a session, querying players, converting bounded to unbounded sessions, and extending a game map) to enhance multiplayer gaming.
Applicant's amended claims are directed towards converting a time bounded gameplay

session, which runs until a predefined game objective is fulfilled or time has expired, to an unbounded gameplay session (in a multiplayer video game), which runs continuously without any set end time, based on a result of a query posed to a predetermined number of the players. If the players show their interest, the time bound (bounded) game is converted to an unbounded gaming session, thereby enhancing the gameplay experience of the players.

The inclusion of automatic monitoring and the transition from bounded to unbounded gameplay sessions is not a mere abstract idea, as it solves a specific, real-world problem in multiplayer gaming-providing greater flexibility in gameplay experiences while synchronizing actions across multiple devices including game servers and client computers connected remotely to said servers.

Further, even if the claim involves an abstract idea, it is patent eligible if it includes an inventive concept sufficient to transform it into a patent-eligible application. Applicant's claims, as amended, recite at least the following specific technological implementation which encompass the inventive concept:

Customization Application: This component runs either on the server computer or on the client computers and automatically monitors gameplay sessions to detect predefined conditions like fulfilling objectives or time expiration. This functionality is highly specific and tied to the operations of the game system.

Gameplay Session Engine: This component runs either on the server computer or on the client computers and performs specialized actions, including: initiating bounded gameplay sessions; querying players dynamically; converting sessions between bounded and unbounded states; extending game maps; and managing session termination based on player participation.

The functionalities implemented by the customization application and the gameplay session engine are not generic but provide a specific sequence of coordinated operations that are tied to the technical architecture of servers and client devices. The automatic conversion of gameplay states, the dynamic extension of game maps, and synchronization across devices involve more than routine or conventional computer functionality.

Applicant submits that in McRO, Inc. v. Bandai Namco Games America, Inc. et al. (Fed. Cir. Sept. 13, 2016), the Federal Circuit held that claims directed to software for automatically animating lip synchronization and facial expressions of animated characters were not directed to an abstract idea under the first prong of the Alice test, and therefore recited patent-eligible subject matter.

The Applicant's claims meet the standards established in McRo v. Bandai Namco Games America, Inc. et al. wherein the Federal Circuit held that claim 1 was "directed to a patentable, technological improvement over the existing, manual 3-D animation techniques" and that claim 1 "uses the limited rules in a process specifically designed to achieve an improved technological result in conventional industry practice."

More specifically, Applicant's claims are directed towards an improvement based on converting a bounded multiplayer video game session to an unbounded video game session based on querying a predefined number of players and it is the claimed alteration of game playing experience, not the implementation of a general purpose computer, that is directed towards improved existing technology, akin to the claims in McRO.

Applicant would further like to draw the Examiner's attention to DDR Holdings, LLC v. Hotels.com, L.P. wherein claims directed to solving an Internet-specific problem by providing a particular technical solution were held patent-eligible.

Applicant's amended claims, similarly, solve a problem unique to multiplayer gaming environments for ensuring seamless transitions between gameplay modes in a distributed system. The claimed combination of features of Applicant's claims meaningfully limit the application of the purported abstract idea in order to solve a problem faced within multi-player video games and/or transform the purported abstract idea into a particular practical application of modulating gameplay experience of one or more players. In particular, Applicant's claims satisfy the requirements of 35 U.S.C. Section 101 at least for the reasons that the claims of DDR Holdings, LLC v. Hotels.com, L.P. were held to satisfy the requirements of 35 USC Section 101.

In keeping with MPEP 2106.05(a), Applicant's amended claims integrates abstract concepts into a specific practical application, as evidenced by its dependence on technological components (e.g., server-based customization application and gameplay session engine).
Hence, Applicant concludes that the amended claims as written are patent eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 because:
* the amended claims are directed to a system and a method which are statutory categories
under § 101;
* the claims are not wholly directed to an abstract idea but rather integrate specific
technological solutions (e.g., automatic monitoring, session conversion, game map
extension) to solve challenges unique to multiplayer video games;
" the claims as presently submitted provide an inventive concept through the
customization application and gameplay session engine, which are specific, unconventional, and directed to improving the operation of multiplayer gaming
systems.

Claims 21-42 stand rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as allegedly being unpatentable over claims 1-20 ofU.S. Patent No. 11,420,119 B2. Applicant is submitting a terminal disclaimer to overcome the rejection. Applicant reserves the right to challenge, and does not waive, the right to challenge the patentably distinct determination in other regulatory or judicial proceedings. Applicant notes that filing a Terminal Disclaimer to obviate a rejection based on non-statutory double patenting does not constitute an admission of the proprietary of the rejection. See Quad Environmental Technologies Corp. v. Union Sanitary District, 946 F.2d 870 (Fed.Cir. 1991) (indicating that "filing of a terminal disclaimer simply serves the statutory function of removing the rejection of double patenting and raises neither a presumption nor estoppel on the merits of the rejection.").

In the interest of clarity and brevity, Applicant may not have addressed every assertion made in the Office Action. Applicant's silence regarding any such assertion does not constitute any admission or acquiescence. Applicant does not admit that any of the cited references or any other references of record is relevant to the present claims, or that they constitute prior art.
